exa-lite.title: US shoppers confront uphill battle in Black Friday discount quest By Reuters
exa-lite.snippet:
LOS ANGELES/RALEIGH, North Carolina, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Inflation-weary US shoppers thronged malls and websites on Black Friday, the traditional kickoff to the holiday spending season, but many said they were struggling to find robust enough bargains to counter the pinch of high gas and grocery prices.

Spending is seen topping last year’s strong results by 4%-6%, and early Black Friday figures point to particularly robust online growth. But brick-and-mortar foot traffic was mixed, and beneath top-line forecasts lie signs of stress.

Most of the gains will be attributable to inflation - which at 3.8% is about a percentage point higher than in each of the last two years - while consumer sentiment remains shaky.

Jasmine Peters, 37, went to the Westfield Century City mall in Los Angeles on Friday hoping to find steeper discounts in-store than online, but they didn’t materialize, and by late morning, she was planning to leave the mall empty-handed. 

Chris Nile, 30, was hoping for more than the $50 discount he saw on a Nintendo Switch 2 gaming console, which brought the price to $450. "Inflation is higher - hell, even the (McDonald’s) McChicken is up," said Nile as he shopped for his two boys at the Crabtree Valley Mall in Raleigh, North Carolina. 

Observers said consumers seemed less impressed by discounts, with stores needing to do more to draw them in. Target Corp, for example, gave away $100 gift cards to the first 100 people in line at each store -- with one lucky recipient receiving a $1,000 card.

"Traffic levels in general seemed off compared to past holidays and seemed to lose steam early," said Michael Brown, Americas retail leader at consulting firm Kearney, who visited several stores in Westchester County, New York, on Friday morning. 

US store visits were tracking 2.4% behind last year’s, at 760 million a little after 6:30 p.m. EST (2330 GMT), according to Passby, a geospatial analytics company that measures real-time foot traffic.

That was the promise when the marketing ploy was popularized in the 1980s, anyway: Americans, still in a festive mood after their Thanksgiving feast and flush with disposable income after several years of economic growth, headed to malls and department stores to begin tackling their Christmas gift lists.
